title: Roman reply A: Vazquez and others call the ban a positive ceremonial law abrogated by the Gospel
source_text: XIV. Ad hoc varia respondent Doctores Scholae Romanae, sed quae refellere difficile non est. Primo enim nonnulli sunt, qui concedunt quidem isto Dei praecepto, omnem prorsus imaginum adorationem & cultum prohiberi, qualiscunque tandem ille sit, ac in eo mentem Dei esse ne ullae effigies, vel alicujus creaturae, vel Dei ipsius colendae proponantur, & modo adorationi accommodato erigantur, atque constituantur. Sed pertendunt istud praeceptum positivum esse & ceremoniale; adeoque fuisse Evangelio abrogatum, ut caetera quae ad ritus legales pertinebant: neque amplius Ecclesiam Christianam eo teneri, & ad observationem ejus esse obstrictam. Haec est sententia Gabrielis Vazquez, quam fuse proponit, & tueri conatur Tomo primo in Tertiam Thomae, Disputatione centesima quarta. Eam quoque amplectitur Lorinus Jesuita scribens in caput decimum septimum Actuum Apostolicorum. Qui in re sequuntur Ambrosium Catharinum, Martinum de Ayala, & Dominicum a Soto, superioris seculi scriptores.
pass_a_gloss: To this the Doctors of the Roman School answer various things, but which it is not difficult to refute. For first there are some who indeed concede that by that commandment of God every adoration and cult of images whatsoever is prohibited, of whatever kind finally it may be, and that in that the mind of God is that no effigies, either of any creature, or of God himself, be proposed to be cultivated, and erected and set up in a mode accommodated to adoration. But they contend that that commandment is positive and ceremonial; and accordingly that it was abrogated by the Gospel, as the other things which pertained to the legal rites: and that the Christian Church is no longer bound by it, and obliged to its observation. This is the opinion of Gabriel Vazquez, which he sets forth at length, and strives to defend, in the first volume on the Third of Thomas, Disputation one hundred four. Lorinus the Jesuit also embraces it, writing on the seventeenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles. Who in the matter follow Ambrosius Catharinus, Martinus de Ayala, and Dominicus a Soto, writers of the former age.
pass_b_english: First Roman escape: grant the ban’s breadth, then reclassify it as positive ceremonial law canceled by the Gospel.
Vazquez (Thomas III, disp. 104) leads; Lorinus, Catharinus, Ayala, and Soto follow.

choices.why: Chief defender of the ceremonial-abrogation view.
